questions.q: What does the lesson mean by a 'traceable' result?
options: Any result produced on real hardware rather than a simulator
A result that was printed to a log file
A result that can be mapped back to the exact git commit, dependency versions, and random seed/shot count that produced it
A result that was shown to a colleague
questions.explain: The lesson defines a traceable result as one where the exact commit, dependencies (Lesson 15), and seed/shots (Lesson 16) that produced it can all be identified -- without that, a reported number is an anecdote, not a reproducible result.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a git tag like `exp-grover-10q-2026-10-18`, as recommended in the lesson?
options: To delete old commits from history
To replace the need for commit messages entirely
To mark the exact commit that produced a specific reported experimental result, retrievable later regardless of how far main has moved
To mark a release version of the software for end users
questions.explain: An experiment tag lets you run `git show exp-grover-10q-2026-10-18` to instantly retrieve the exact code snapshot behind a specific reported number, even after the main branch has changed substantially since.

questions.q: Why does the lesson's .gitignore example explicitly un-ignore `tests/fixtures/expected_counts/*.json` even while ignoring `results/raw_counts/*.json`?
options: Because fixture files are always larger than raw result dumps
Because small, hand-curated golden result files are part of what makes a regression test's claims checkable later, while large raw dumps don't belong in git at all
Because raw counts and golden fixtures are functionally identical and the distinction doesn't matter
Because .gitignore cannot exclude JSON files
questions.explain: Raw per-shot dumps from large sweeps are bulky and not meant to live in git, but small curated golden files that tests compare against are essential, checked-in parts of the test suite -- losing them to an overly broad gitignore rule would silently weaken testing.

questions.q: What three things does the lesson's example commit message do that a terse message like 'fixed oracle' does not?
options: List every file changed in the repository
Explain the bug mechanism, point to the specific test that caught it, and flag which previously-tagged results are now suspect
Nothing extra -- both messages convey the same information
Automatically revert the previous commit
questions.explain: The lesson's example commit message explains why the bug occurred (swapped control/target qubits), names the test that caught it, and explicitly calls out that a previously tagged, previously-reported result is now invalid -- information a one-line message would lose entirely.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a git tag alone doesn't guarantee a result is fully reproducible?
options: Because git tags are deleted automatically after 90 days
Because tags only work with GitHub, not other git hosts
Because reproducibility is impossible for quantum code in principle

Because reproducing the result also requires the exact dependency versions to still resolve (Lesson 15) and the exact random seed/shot count to be recorded (Lesson 16) -- a tag only identifies the code
questions.explain: A tag identifies which code produced a result, but re-running that exact code still needs its dependencies to be pinned and resolvable (Lesson 15) and its random seed/shot count recorded (Lesson 16) -- all three together are what full reproducibility requires.
